**The Orchard in My City**

When I first stepped onto the cracked sidewalk of the old railway line that ran through the heart of our city, the world as I had known it—a grid of glass towers, the constant hiss of streetcars, the chatter of commuters—was suddenly interrupted by something different: a smell, sharp and sweet, that made my eyes water. It was the scent of apples, nuts, and soil that had never been part of the city's perfume until then. The air was cooler, too, as if the invisible walls of a greenhouse had replaced the barbed expectations of concrete and steel.

On the first day, I didn't think much of it. I had once been a city-watcher, a person who walked the streets taking snapshots in mind of the odd faces that read books on moonlit benches, of trains that never seemed to stop for people, of the way rain trickled off a diddle of tile. But that morning, I slipped into the narrow alley that had, until then, been a forgotten passageway for the sort of people who lived behind the old brick walls and did not forget their keys.

That alley took me on a hidden path, winding past an old Masonic lodge, a sun‑shining laundromat, and a small swing on a cracked porch. I could see it from the outside: a patch of light; a single, ivy‑clad fence. And when I went inside, the world changed again. Shadows were deeper. A soft thrum, the whisper of wind through leaves, breaking the city’s usual drone. And the orchard was there—tiny, but green and alive. Apples hung proudly on branches, black and blue, huge compared to the vision that had been in my mind before the moment it had finally materialized.

I had a memory of apples that tasted like summer, of summers that stretched across a horizon of pine needles and the taste of rain turned inside the city. Those apples had always been a taste of my childhood, a memory of my father’s laugh. He always said it was all in the world: All it took one object to capture the whole. So I couldn’t help but let something bloom from this moment. In the orchard, I found a quiet door in the conversation between city and nature.
